summary: Specifies the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, which gives access to the X.500 Directory without the heavy requirements of the full Directory Access Protocol. It targets simple management and browser applications. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3494.

eli5.summary: A lighter way to look things up in a big online directory, like a quick phone book lookup.

questions: how do i search an x.500 directory
subtitle: A lightweight protocol for directory lookups and management without the overhead of full X.500.

tldr.problem: X.500 directories are powerful but require heavy protocol machinery and complex client implementations. Many applications need simple directory access for reading and writing information without that complexity.
tldr.mechanism: LDAP adds a lightweight protocol layer over TCP that strips away the presentation and session overheads of the full Directory Access Protocol (DAP). Clients send requests to servers over TCP, and servers handle the directory operations, returning results.
tldr.outcome: LDAP made directory services practical for browsers and management applications, but RFC 1777 (version 2) was soon superseded by RFC 3494 (version 3) to address limitations found in early deployment.

today: RFC 1777 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 3494 (LDAPv3), which addressed limitations and became the standard for directory access.

sections.title: Lightweight Access to X.500
sections.content:
RFC 1777 specifies the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), a way to access the X.500 Directory without the resource requirements of the full Directory Access Protocol (DAP). The RFC is targeted at simple management applications and browser applications that perform interactive access to the directory.

The key innovation is stripping away the session and presentation layers that DAP uses. Instead of encoding protocol elements in complex abstract syntax notation, LDAP carries them directly over TCP as straightforward data structures, making client and server implementations simpler.
sections.eli5: LDAP is a simpler way to ask a directory server questions. You don't need heavy machinery; just connect and ask.

sections.title: Client-Server Model
sections.content:
LDAP uses a simple client-server model where clients send protocol requests to servers, and servers return responses containing results or errors. This model minimizes client complexity to enable widespread deployment.

A client must first issue a Bind operation to authenticate and start a session. Servers are not required to enforce strict ordering of requests and responses; clients may send multiple requests and receive responses in any order, as long as each request eventually receives a response. Servers handle all directory operations on behalf of clients, including following referrals internally, so clients see only final results.
sections.eli5: One client talks to one server. The client says what it wants, and the server does the work and tells the client the answer.

sections.title: Messages and Data Structures
sections.content:
All LDAP protocol operations are wrapped in a common LDAPMessage envelope containing a message ID and a protocol operation (such as a BindRequest, SearchRequest, or ModifyRequest). The message ID is echoed back in responses and allows clients to match responses to requests.

Strings such as Distinguished Names are encoded as plain strings rather than complex ASN.1 types. The protocol uses a lightweight BER (Basic Encoding Rules) encoding that is simpler than the full X.690 standard. Operation results are returned using an LDAPResult structure containing a result code, matched DN (for searches), and an optional human-readable error message.
sections.eli5: Every message has a number so you know which answer goes with which question. Names are written as readable text, not in a secret code.

sections.title: Core Operations
sections.content:
The Bind operation authenticates the client and establishes a session. It specifies a version number (this RFC is version 2), a distinguished name to authenticate as (or null for anonymous access), and authentication credentials. Simple authentication passes a cleartext password; Kerberos version 4 credentials are also supported.

The Search operation is the most commonly used. It specifies a base object (the starting point in the directory tree), a scope (baseObject, singleLevel, or wholeSubtree), and a filter expression using equality, substring, greater-than, less-than, and other matching rules. The Unbind operation closes the session.

Modification operations (Add, Modify, Delete, ModifyRDN, Compare) allow clients to change directory entries. All operations follow the same request-response pattern through the LDAPMessage envelope.
sections.eli5: Bind says who you are. Search finds things. Add, Modify, and Delete change things. Each operation sends a message and waits for a reply.

sections.title: Transport and Deployment
sections.content:
LDAP messages are carried directly over TCP (port 389 is the standard server port) or over a connection-oriented transport service. The protocol requires reliable delivery and that all 8 bits of an octet be preserved during transmission.

The design goal was to complement, not replace, the full DAP. LDAP provides a strict subset of the Directory abstract service, so a DAP server can implement LDAP directly. This RFC is Historic: version 3 (RFC 3494) addressed limitations discovered in early deployments and became the widely used standard. Among the improvements in v3 were better authentication support, UTF-8 string handling, and protocol extensions via controls.
sections.eli5: LDAP runs over plain TCP on port 389. You connect, send messages, and get answers back. Version 2 was later improved in version 3.
